title: Code Example
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
System.out.println("a == b : " + (a == b));  // false
        System.out.println("a != b : " + (a != b));  // true
        System.out.println("a >  b : " + (a >  b));  // false
        System.out.println("a <  b : " + (a <  b));  // true
        System.out.println("a >= b : " + (a >= b));  // false
        System.out.println("a <= b : " + (a <= b));  // true
    }
}
```

**Output:**
```
a == b : false
a != b : true
a >  b : false
a <  b : true
a >= b : false
a <= b : true
```

title: Increment & Decrement — Prefix vs Postfix
subtitle: This is a very common interview topic and source of confusion.
bullets: This is a **very common interview topic** and source of confusion.
code:
Step 1: Return current value of a
Step 2: Then increment (or decrement) a

title: Code Example — Step by Step
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
// POSTFIX increment: return 5, then a becomes 6
        System.out.println(a++);  // prints 5   (a is now 6)

// PREFIX increment: a becomes 7, then return 7
        System.out.println(++a);  // prints 7   (a is now 7)

// POSTFIX decrement: return 7, then a becomes 6
        System.out.println(a--);  // prints 7   (a is now 6)

// PREFIX decrement: a becomes 5, then return 5
        System.out.println(--a);  // prints 5   (a is now 5)

title: Overview
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Shift operators move all bits of a number **left** or **right** by a specified number of positions. They are essentially very fast **multiplication or division by powers of 2**.

title: Three Types
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
| Operator | Symbol | Name | Effect |
|----------|--------|------|--------|
| Left shift | `<<` | Signed left shift | Shift bits left; fill right with `0` |
| Right shift | `>>` | Signed right shift | Shift bits right; fill left with **sign bit** |
| Unsigned right shift | `>>>` | Unsigned right shift | Shift bits right; fill left with `0` always |

title: 9.1 Left Shift (`<<`)
subtitle: ### How It Works
bullets: Shift all bits to the **left** by `n` positions.
The rightmost vacated positions are **always filled with `0`**.
code: a << n  ≡  a × 2^n

title: 9.2 Signed Right Shift (`>>`)
subtitle: ### How It Works
bullets: Shift all bits to the **right** by `n` positions.
The leftmost vacated positions are filled with the **sign bit** (MSB):
code: a >> n  ≡  a / 2^n   (for positive numbers)

title: 9.3 Unsigned Right Shift (`>>>`)
subtitle: ### How It Works
bullets: Shift all bits to the **right** by `n` positions.
The leftmost vacated positions are **always filled with `0`**, regardless of the sign bit.
code:
a = -5  →  1111 1011

a >>> 1:   shift right by 1
            0111 1101  = 125
            ↑ always filled with 0 — sign NOT preserved

title: What is Precedence?
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
Because `*` has **higher precedence** than `+`, the multiplication happens first:
```
5 + (2 * 3) = 5 + 6 = 11
```

title: What is Associativity?
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
Example:
```java
10 * 5 / 2
```
Both `*` and `/` have the same precedence. Their associativity is **left-to-right**, so:
```
(10 * 5) / 2 = 50 / 2 = 25
```

title: Java Operator Precedence Table
subtitle: (Higher row = Higher precedence = Evaluated first)
bullets:
| Priority | Category | Operators | Associativity |
|----------|----------|-----------|---------------|
| 1 (Highest) | Postfix | `expr++`, `expr--` | Left → Right |
| 2 | Unary prefix | `++expr`, `--expr`, `+expr`, `-expr`, `~`, `!` | Right → Left |
| 3 | Multiplicative | `*`, `/`, `%` | Left → Right |
| 4 | Additive | `+`, `-` | Left → Right |
| 5 | Shift | `<<`, `>>`, `>>>` | Left → Right |
| 6 | Relational | `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `instanceof` | Left → Right |
| 7 | Equality | `==`, `!=` | Left → Right |
| 8 | Bitwise AND | `&` | Left → Right |
| 9 | Bitwise XOR | `^` | Left → Right |
| 10 | Bitwise OR | `\|` | Left → Right |
| 11 | Logical AND | `&&` | Left → Right |
| 12 | Logical OR | `\|\|` | Left → Right |
| 13 | Ternary | `?
code:
> int result = (5 + 2) * 3;   // clearly 21
> int result = 5 + (2 * 3);   // clearly 11
>

title: The Strategy
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: When you encounter a complex expression with `++`, `--`, and multiple operators, follow this process:
**Identify and substitute all operand current values** (handle postfix: return value first, then update; handle prefix: update first, then return value).

title: Worked Example from the Lecture
subtitle: ### Step 1: Substitute Operand Values
bullets: Track `a`'s value as you go left to right:

| Token | Current `a` | Action | Value Used | `a` after |
|-------|------------|--------|------------|-----------|
| `a++` | 4 | Postfix: use 4, then a++ | **4** | 5 |
| `++a` | 5 | Prefix: a++ first → 6, then use 6 | **6** | 6 |
| `--a` | 6 | Prefix: a-- first → 5, then use 5 | **5** | 5 |
| `a--` | 5 | Postfix: use 5, then a-- | **5** | 4 |
code:
int a = 4;
int result = a++ + ++a * --a + a--;

title: Mistake 2: Integer Division Surprise
subtitle: Fix: Use double:

title: Mistake 3: Confusing Postfix and Prefix in Expressions
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Many beginners assume `a++` increments before the assignment. It does not — the assignment gets the old value.

title: Mistake 4: Expecting `~n` to Give the Bitwise Complement as Positive
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Java uses signed two's complement — `~n` always gives `-(n+1)`, not just a bit flip to a positive number.
code:
int a = 4;
System.out.println(~a);  // prints -5, NOT 3

title: Mistake 5: Using `>>` instead of `>>>` for Unsigned Shift
subtitle: If you want to treat bits as unsigned, always use >>>.
bullets: If you want to treat bits as unsigned, always use `>>>`.

title: Mistake 6: Precedence Assumption Without Parentheses
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: While this happens to be correct, always use parentheses to make intent explicit.

title: Mistake 7: `instanceof` on `null`
subtitle: Conceptual Details
code:
Object obj = null;
System.out.println(obj instanceof String);  // false — does NOT throw NullPointerException
